question: Your company has a December year-end. One peer reports to 31 March: EBITDA was £80m in the year to March 2026 and is forecast at £96m in the year to March 2027. What is the peer's calendar-2026 EBITDA?
model_answer_md:
Calendar 2026 runs January–December 2026. The peer's two financial years split it:

- **January–March 2026** is the last 3 months of the year to March 2026
- **April–December 2026** is the first 9 months of the year to March 2027

Weight each year by the months it contributes (assuming profit is earned evenly through the year):

$$0.25 \times £80\text{m} + 0.75 \times £96\text{m} = £20\text{m} + £72\text{m} = \mathbf{£92\text{m}}$$

Without this step you would compare your company's calendar-2026 multiple with the peer's year to March 2026 — a period mostly in 2025 — and a growing peer would look more expensive than it is.
key_points: Calendar 2026 = 3 months of FY to Mar-26 + 9 months of FY to Mar-27
Without it, multiples compare different periods

follow_ups.question: What if the business is seasonal?
follow_ups.answer_md: Simple time-weighting assumes profit is earned evenly. For a seasonal business, such as a retailer earning most of its profit at Christmas, use the quarterly or half-year figures it reports to build the calendar year from the actual periods.

follow_ups.question: Is this the same as an LTM figure?
follow_ups.answer_md: Related but different. LTM (last twelve months) adds the latest interim period to the last annual figure and strips out the matching prior-year period, giving the most recent actual 12 months. Calendarisation lines up forecasts or actuals to a common year-end.

weak_answer_note: Using the peer's financial-year figure unadjusted, or weighting the years the wrong way round.
